## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sīlavīmaṁsajātaka* (Ja 330) is a narrative in the Pali *Jātaka* collection, situated as the tenth discourse in the *Kuṭidūsakavagga* [Fausböll 1883]. In his discussion of Buddhist narrative headings, J. S. Speyer observes that titles such as *Sīlavīmaṁsajātaka* illustrate tales named after an action—namely the testing or examination of moral virtue—rather than a person or object [Speyer 1895].

According to the canonical commentary, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana with reference to a brahmin who repeatedly tested his own virtue [Fausböll 1883]. While noting that two similar stories had been related previously, this birth-story recounts an occasion in Benares when the Bodhisatta was the king's royal chaplain (*purohita*) [Fausböll 1883]. Seeking to determine whether he is honoured for his virtue or for other qualities, the Bodhisatta takes coins from a money-changer over three consecutive days until he is apprehended [Fausböll 1883]. Recognizing the supreme preeminence of moral conduct (*sīla*), he subsequently renounces worldly life, takes up the ascetic life of a seer (*isipabbajjā*) in the forest, attains the meditative absorptions and higher spiritual knowledges (*jhānābhiññā*), and is ultimately reborn in the Brahmā world [Fausböll 1883]. At the conclusion of the teaching, the Buddha identifies the royal chaplain as an earlier incarnation of himself [Fausböll 1883].
